Artificial intelligence and digital 
inequalities: new challenges for Poland
Date of submission: 09.03.2025; date of acceptance: 30.05.2025 
JEL classification: L16, L17, O14, O38.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, digital inequalities, Poland
Abstract
The article deals with the problem of digital inequalities that may develop in Poland due to the wide-
spread introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) in all areas of contemporary social and economic 
life. In addition to the existing forms of digital inequalities, new ones are emerging, related to the 
dominance of a group of countries with the highest technological level, which are able to effective-
ly impose new standards of economic and social development. New forms of digital inequalities, 
emerging alongside the rapid development of AI, go beyond the traditional issues of Internet con-
nectivity or hardware availability. They include disparities in access to the high-quality training 
data, limited national capacities to develop and deploy large language models (LLMs), unequal 
availability of high-performance computing infrastructure, and gaps in algorithmic transparency 
as well as AI governance. The concise analysis presented in this article aims at indicating the strat-
egies that Poland has implemented in the third decade of the 21st century to enable the inclusive 
development of AI at the national level. The research explores how Poland’s national AI strategy 
can address internal barriers — such as underdeveloped infrastructure, limited computing capacity, 
and uneven distribution of digital skills — to promote more inclusive and equitable AI develop-
ment. The central research question is: What strategic actions should Poland undertake to ensure 
a more inclusive development of artificial intelligence. The analysis uses a descriptive method to 
understand the factors that have a particular impact on the occurrence of digital inequalities in 
Poland. The results of the study show that Poland still faces many technological delays, including 
those in the implementation of AI solutions. This may result in a deepening of digital inequalities 
in the sphere of business as well as society. One strategy that seems to have the greatest positive 
impact on the inclusive development of AI is national and international cooperation between the 
public and private sectors in this area.

1. Introduction
The development of digital technologies in the 21st century is gaining exceptional 
momentum, and one of its key drivers is artificial intelligence (AI). Its application 
spans almost all areas of social and economic life, from industry to education, as 
well as public administration and medical services. The increasing implementa-
tion of AI is helping to make business processes more efficient, optimise work 
and generate innovative solutions. However, despite the numerous benefits, the 
massive implementation of AI also reveals new challenges, including the emer-
gence and deepening of digital inequalities. Traditional forms of digital inequal-
ities have been primarily related to limited access to technological infrastructure, 
lack of digital competence and economic barriers. However, new aspects of this 
phenomenon are emerging in the age of AI. Access to the advanced AI systems, 
high-quality data, and computing power is becoming more diverse globally, which 
can lead to inequalities between high-tech and developing countries. Furthermore, 
the AI algorithms may reinforce already existing social inequalities through chan-
ges in decision-making patterns or differences in access to advanced technologies.
The aim of this article is to explore the main challenges associated with pro-
moting an inclusive approach to artificial intelligence (AI) development in Poland, 
particularly in the context of digital inequalities emerging from the global spread 
of AI technologies. New forms of digital inequalities, emerging alongside the rapid 
development of AI, go beyond traditional issues of Internet connectivity or hard-
ware availability. They include disparities in access to high-quality training data, 
limited national capacities to develop and deploy large language models (LLMs), 
unequal availability of high-performance computing infrastructure, and gaps in 
algorithmic transparency and AI governance.
The analysis focuses on identifying the key drivers that contribute to the deep-
ening of AI-related inequalities and examines their economic and social implica-
tions, especially in the contrast between highly developed countries — setting 
global technological standards — and Poland, which faces specific structural and 
infrastructural barriers. The study places particular emphasis on the role of inter-
national cooperation as a mechanism to enhance access to emerging technologies. 
Moreover, it investigates whether reducing digital inequalities in Poland is inher-
ently tied to the formulation and implementation of a comprehensive AI develop-
ment strategy — one that includes building adequate infrastructure, strengthening 
computing capacity, and improving the digital competencies of the population. 
The central research question guiding this study is: What strategic actions 
should Poland undertake to ensure a more inclusive development of artificial in-
telligence, and to what extent can international cooperation, infrastructure invest-
ment, and digital skill enhancement mitigate emerging digital inequalities in the 
AI era?


Artificial intelligence and digital inequalities: new challenges for Poland	
101
2. Theoretical framework of the research
In the scientific literature, the concept of artificial intelligence (Bjola, 2021) is de-
fined in a wide variety of ways, from stating that it is a computer programme ca-
pable of executing commands that require similar intelligence to that of a human 
being; to an elaborate characterisation of trained algorithms. This includes skills 
such as pattern recognition, natural language processing, machine learning, deci-
sion-making and the ability to adapt and self-learn (Russell, Norvig, 2020). AI can 
be classified on different levels of sophistication, from narrow artificial intelligence 
(ANI) systems that are specialised in a single task (e.g. medical image analysis) to 
a general artificial intelligence (AGI), which could — in the future — match hu-
man intelligence in a wide range of tasks (Goertzel, 2014).
Work on artificial intelligence has been carried out intensively since the second 
half of the 20th century. It was mainly in the context of academic research with 
a limited application scope. In 2016, the US-based artificial intelligence research 
laboratory Open AI released for the public use a software platform for measuring 
and training the AI general intelligence. A few years later, further language mod-
els were made available to interpret commands given in natural language and to 
process questions and answers. With these models it was possible to solve different 
types of problems, especially in science, programming and reasoning. However, 
it is only with the advent of language models, developed and refined by Open AI 
and then by corporations such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and making them 
available to the general public, that a new chapter in the history of technological 
progress can be considered to have begun. It represents a continuation of the de-
velopment processes of the information and communication technology sector. 
At the same time, the scale and scope of the new technology, which is the use of 
computer systems for information processing, problem-solving reasoning and de-
cision-making, affects the whole of social, political and economic life to an un-
precedented extent. This is reflected in the enormous interest in this technology and 
the number of studies and analyses undertaken by specialists representing many 
scientific disciplines (Shaheen, 2024; Ragnedda, Gladkova, 2020; Helsper, 2021). 
In parallel with the publications of well-known research centres, universities and 
teams working on the implementation of artificial intelligence in the business sec-
tor, there are reports from international organisations. These describe the positive 
and negative sides of successive applications of artificial intelligence and their ef-
fects on many areas of social life and individuals. 
Thanks to AI, widespread changes are taking place in the ability to innov-
ate at the micro level — from small businesses to multinational corporations to 
the macro level of countries. AI is also determining new forms and areas of inter-
national competitiveness. However, it also brings with it major risks associated 
with its use as an instrument of pressure (soft power). The introduction of artificial 


102	
Karolina Olszewska-Ziemba
intelligence is setting in motion particularly fierce competition between countries, 
especially in the areas of IT infrastructure of the information and communica-
tion technology industry. Few economies in the world have the right conditions 
for working on AI technology. The process of moving from laboratory research 
to widespread applications has been possible in countries with a cadre of highly 
specialised research skills and adequate infrastructure for the production of spe-
cialised processors. These factors have raised the competitive struggle in the global 
economy to a higher level.
The analysis of the changes that the application of artificial intelligence has 
brought to competitiveness, broadly defined, is dealt with by numerous reports 
from public and private institutions ( Organization for Economic Co-operation 
and Development, 2024). Basically, most of them refer to the characteristics of 
the markets for AI industry infrastructure components. The European Union has 
paid particular attention to the ethical issues of AI applications. It outlined these 
issues in a piece of legislation issued in 2024, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act 
(European Parliament, 2024). This step was taken shortly after AI language mod-
els produced by major US companies entered the market. In the global market, 
only a dozen companies from highly developed countries produce processors ca-
pable of performing complex operations in the area of neural network training. 
This market is highly competitive and leadership positions are difficult to maintain 
in the long term. The constant race by highly innovative players to gain a leader-
ship position is causing an extraordinary dynamism in the AI industry on the one 
hand, but a widening digital gap between countries on the other. The introduction 
of artificial intelligence is setting in motion a particularly fierce competition in the 
global AI market, especially in the areas of IT infrastructure of the information and 
communication technology industry. Countries that do not have sufficient resour-
ces to develop their own language models and AI solutions are unable to maintain 
digital sovereignty, resulting in digital inequalities.
Digital inequalities are a manifestation of broader economic and social in-
equalities. They encompass not only the lack of access to digital infrastructure 
but also insufficient digital skills, which are essential for fully utilizing technol-
ogy and integrating into the digital society (Olszewska, 2020; Robinson et al., 
2015) Digital inequalities in the national economy can occur in various forms. 
It emerges primarily in businesses, in their uneven capacity to innovate, absorb 
knowledge and continuously implement new techniques in the production pro-
cess. These differences particularly affect the SME sector. These factors result in 
companies having unequal opportunities to compete, not only in the domestic but 
especially in the international market. This is particularly true of the introduction 
of new technology such as artificial intelligence into their processes. The auto-
mation of processes at different levels of companies and the general streamlining 
of employees’ activities brings productivity gains and other benefits. Their abil-
ity to master complex situations increases, thanks not only to repetitive activities 


Artificial intelligence and digital inequalities: new challenges for Poland	
103
but also to various platforms that allow them to master more complex and unique 
activities. The greater the pool of employees capable of rapidly absorbing and dif-
fusing knowledge to master unique processes, the more the company’s potential 
to compete in the marketplace increases. As a result, the international competi-
tiveness of the economy also increases. 
Countries in the global market have unequal historical backgrounds, material 
resources and skilled workers and managers. This translates into the technological 
level of the existing production and social structure. In an environment of rapid 
technological progress requiring the maximum commitment of forces and capital, 
the forefront of countries able to develop and implement AI solutions on a large 
scale is coming to the fore. As in previous eras, there is a process of partial ex-
clusion of some national economies from the processes of adopting and reaping 
the benefits of technological progress. To an even greater extent than was the case 
in previous industrial revolutions, there is a division of the world economy into 
developed countries and countries unable to keep up with new trends in techno-
logical development.
3. Research methodology
The adopted research methodology made it possible to identify the challenges 
currently faced by the Polish economy in the context of the global development of 
artificial intelligence and to identify potential paths for minimising the negative 
effects of digital inequalities in Poland.
A descriptive method was adopted as the main research method to analyse 
existing data and literature on the impact of artificial intelligence on the labour 
market and global resources. Scientific publications, statistical data and reports 
from international and Polish institutions and organisations were analysed. This 
allowed for an understanding of general trends and relationships in the area of the 
impact of AI on the problem of digital inequalities. 
Until 2022, AI research concentrated on laboratory settings, with practical 
implementations occurring on a relatively limited scale. However, the rapid emer-
gence of large language models (LLMs) marks the onset of a broad technological 
revolution, the full implications of which are still unfolding. At this formative 
stage of AI development; key concepts, definitions, and statistical categories are 
still being shaped and standardized. As a result, a descriptive and qualitative ap-
proach is the most appropriate methodological choice, as it allows for the explora-
tion and contextualization of emerging trends, social impacts, and policy challen-
ges in a flexible and interpretive manner. While quantitative data — particularly 
those relating to hardware capabilities or software usage — can serve as a valuable 
complement, such data alone are insufficient to capture the multidimensional na-
ture of AI’s development and its broader socio-economic implications (Jariwala, 


104	
Karolina Olszewska-Ziemba
2024). Therefore, this study uses descriptive analysis to provide a better under-
standing of the dynamics and consequences of AI implementation in its current 
state of evolution.
The study tries to identify necessary elements in an inclusive AI development 
strategy in Poland in the first half of the third decade of the 21st century to contrib-
ute to the reduction of digital inequalities. Poland was selected as en example due 
to the fact that it is the largest economy among the member states, and it was ad-
mitted to the EU in 2004. Poland can, therefore, serve as a representative example 
to better understand other Central and Eastern European economies that also face 
the problem of digital inequalities and technological lag vis-à-vis Western Euro-
pean countries, the United States and a group of technologically developed Asian 
countries, referred to as the “Asian tigers”.
4. Digital inequalities in Poland in the context of the 
global AI development
Artificial intelligence plays a key role in economic and social transformation. On 
the one hand, it brings numerous benefits, such as increasing productivity, improv-
ing the quality of goods and services, and supporting the development of innov-
ation. On the other hand, its uneven deployment can lead to new forms of digital 
inequalities, affecting the distribution of global resources, the shaping of techno-
logical standards and the structure of the labour market. Unequal opportunities for 
the development of AI arise from the requirements of, among other things, hav-
ing very large energy resources to power AI centres, access to rare metals used in 
computer technology, and a highly educated workforce familiar with technologic-
al, economic, social, and environmental aspects. These elements result in a group 
of highly developed countries coming out on top in the AI technology race at the 
very start.
Given that artificial intelligence is becoming a key factor influencing the re-
distribution of global technological, capital and knowledge resources, and taking 
into account the strategic official plans for AI development in Poland (Ministerstwo 
Cyfryzacji, Ministerstwo Przedsiębiorczości i Technologii, Ministerstwo Nauki 
i Szkolnictwa Wyższego, Ministerstwo Inwestycji i Rozwoju, 2019), this country 
faces four main challenges in relation to this fact:
1. Inequalities in access to AI technologies between Poland and digitally ad-
vanced countries: Highly developed countries such as the US, China and Western 
European countries (mainly Sweden, Germany, France, and the UK) have a techno-
logical advantage due to their access to advanced AI systems, high-quality data 
and computing resources (Paz, 2020). Poland, on the other hand, lagging behind the 
West in terms of AI development, often lacks an adequately developed digital, in-
stitutional, educational and financial infrastructure, leading to new forms of digital 


Artificial intelligence and digital inequalities: new challenges for Poland	
105
inequalities. As artificial intelligence becomes a key factor in the global economy, 
the inequality in AI investment between developed countries and Poland is also 
growing. Developed countries are investing huge sums in research, development, 
and commercialisation of AI technologies, allowing them to increase their techno-
logical resources further. In China, according to a McKinsey & Company’s (2018) 
report, investments in AI have reached billions of dollars, and the country aims to 
dominate the global AI market by 2030. In Poland, on the other hand, investments 
in AI are limited due to a lack of access to capital and technological resources. 
The lack of adequate funding for development, as well as institutional and social 
barriers, may significantly delay Poland’s integration into the global development 
of AI technologies (Brynjolfsson, McAfee, 2014).
2. Monopolisation of AI by global technology corporations: Global technol-
ogy companies such as Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI dominate the field of AI, 
controlling key artificial intelligence algorithms and platforms (Zuboff, 2019). The 
concentration of digital innovation in the hands of a few players limits access to 
advanced technologies for smaller companies and academic and public institu-
tions, which may lead to uneven economic development between Poland and the 
leaders in AI. Increased analysis and processing of information is also associated 
with inequalities in the areas of privacy, algorithmic ethics and the threat of poten-
tial misuse of data by corporations and government institutions of technologically 
dominant countries. Poland released a new PLLuM language model in 2024, dedi-
cated to public administration, businesses, and academia, as a response to prod-
ucts such as ChatGPT and DeepSeek. However, the Polish language model eco-
system is only in its infancy and is not able to compete in the global LLM (Large 
Language Model) market. Nevertheless, it is important that the development of the 
Polish AI ecosystem is a crucial step towards building Poland’s digital sovereignty.
3. Exploitation of AI resources and energy: Training AI models requires enor-
mous computing power and access to data, which involves significant energy con-
sumption (Desislavov et al., 2023). Poland faces limited energy resources and 
a weaker digital infrastructure compared to AI leaders worldwide, exacerbating 
its marginalisation in the global technology ecosystem.
4. Market segmentation and social inequalities: Increasing automation is lead-
ing to a polarised labour market. The increasing demand for highly skilled AI pro-
fessionals contrasts with a decreasing number of jobs for people performing low-
paid, routine tasks. Such a process can exacerbate social inequalities and lead to 
an increase in labour precarisation, i.e. employment with low stability and social 
security (Acemoglu, Restrepo, 2020). Poland has made progress in digitalisation 
in recent years but still ranks below the EU average. In the 2022 DESI — Digital 
Economy and Society Index, Poland ranked 24th out of 27 EU Member States. The 
2024 National Report on the Digital Decade in Poland highlighted one of the lead-
ing causes of digital inequalities in Poland, which is the lack of basic digital skills. 
The percentage of the population with at least basic digital skills is below the EU

to be more than five times higher than the average observed in recent years to reach

criteria of strategic importance for the development of artificial intelligence were

107
5. Strategies for a more inclusive development of AI 
in Poland  
Considering the dynamics of AI development in the world, including in the de-
veloped economies of EU member states in Western Europe, Poland has the task 
of effectively implementing solutions that will enable more inclusive AI develop-
ment at the level of the national economy. According to Sala and Tańska (2024, 
109), there are many important reasons to conclude that Poland is on the “wrong 
track” of technological development, based on the authors’ retrospective analysis. 
Poland is struggling with a technological lag stemming from the communist era in 
the form of a generation gap and a lack of sufficient high-class analysts and design-
ers of information systems and artificial intelligence solutions. The competence 
gap in the area of digital technologies is still present. The fundamental problem 
of Poland is the issue of reforming programmes at universities, which so far have 
not been able to catch up with the aforementioned delays, taking into account the 
competitive advantage in education systems in countries highly advanced in AI 
development. The solution seems to be the creation of an institutional framework 
that will allow for the implementation of modern education programmes, as imple-
mented in the USA, in the Scandinavian countries, including the so-called Swed-
ish model, the UK and the Netherlands, as well as in Southeast Asian countries 
such as the Republic of Korea, Singapore and China. In these countries, innova-
tion ecosystems that combine science and industry are highly developed, which 
results in the inclusive development of AI.
Therefore, the task for the coming decades is to implement an inclusive AI de-
velopment strategy in Poland that will provide effective and comprehensive support 
for education, science, business, and international cooperation, with an emphasis 
on the ethical and responsible use of technology. In 2020, Poland adopted the In-
tegrated Skills Strategy 2030 in a resolution of the Council of Ministers. However, 
its effective implementation faces many obstacles, such as an insufficient number 
of teaching staff prepared to transfer knowledge adequate to the new conditions 
of AI development.
It should be emphasised that the inclusive development of AI requires the in-
volvement of all entities of the triple helix as a model of cooperation between sci-
ence, administration and business so that the benefits of AI are available to all cit-
izens. One of the objectives should also be to create institutional conditions that, 
through funding mechanisms for innovative Polish AI solutions and for innovative 
enterprises, will strengthen the diffusion of digital technologies and support the 
development of digital competencies, both in the private sector (especially SMEs) 
and in society as a whole.
In 2020, one of the key documents containing a strategic framework for the 
inclusive development of AI was published: “A policy for the development of 


108	
Karolina Olszewska-Ziemba
artificial intelligence in Poland from 2020”, which defines actions in the short-
term (until 2023), medium-term (until 2027) and long-term (after 2027). Six areas 
have been identified within the framework of this policy (Ministerstwo Cyfry-
zacji, 2020, 6–7):
1. AI and society: It is defined as the first and priority area. The goal is to make 
Poland one of the primary beneficiaries of the data-driven economy and to pro-
mote the need for citizens to continuously improve their digital skills. Activities 
in this area focus on supporting the development of open technology platforms 
and data resources, which can help reduce inequalities. One example is the Open 
Data initiative, which promotes the sharing of public data in a transparent man-
ner and makes it accessible to everyone. In Poland, the definition of Open Data is 
included in the Act of 11 August 2021 on open data and the reuse of public sector 
information. Thanks to this initiative, companies and other organisations will be 
able to use open access to data to develop their own applications and AI solutions. 
Enabling wider access to data resources and AI algorithms can also contribute to 
the development of digital innovations in SMEs and start-ups that do not have the 
same resources as large corporations.
2. AI and innovative companies: The measures taken are aimed at supporting 
Polish AI companies, creating mechanisms to finance their development and pro-
moting cooperation between start-ups and the public sector. The Polish government 
should focus on developing policies to support small and medium-sized enterprises 
(SMEs) in the integration of AI, as well as on ensuring that these technologies do 
not lead to new forms of exclusion. One example of this is considering mandatory 
regulations for algorithm transparency and mandatory auditing of AI technologies 
to ensure they are accessible and fair to all users. In addition to the aforementioned 
support framework, the creation of AI regulations that promote equal access to 
technology for entrepreneurs is of great importance for practical cooperation be-
tween the private and public sectors.
3. AI and science: The strategic objective of this component is to support the 
scientific community in designing interdisciplinary AI solutions. There is a need 
for greater involvement of specialists from the humanities and social sciences ca-
pable of creating an ethical and safe framework for AI technologies. An interdisci-
plinary approach is essential to solving the complex challenges posed by artificial 
intelligence, ensuring that its development is in line with social values and ethical 
standards. The social acceptance of AI technology depends on whether people 
perceive it as fair, transparent and ethically sound. An interdisciplinary approach, 
therefore, allows for the development of AI that is better understood and accepted 
by society (Rahwan et al., 2019). The combination of representatives of the exact 
sciences with representatives of the humanities and social sciences in research 
work will enable the design of technologies that are more just, useful and in line 
with social values. The integration of the humanities and social sciences with tech-
nology ensures that AI will be a tool to support people, not a threat to society. The 


Artificial intelligence and digital inequalities: new challenges for Poland	
109
Polish science system is undergoing transformation, but on a larger scale, there 
is a lack of scientific projects that would solve complex ethical and legal issues 
in the process of AI implementation. The development of AI involves significant 
moral and social dilemmas, such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the impact 
of automation on the labour market. Philosophy, ethics and sociology help to iden-
tify and address these challenges, ensuring that AI develops in a responsible way 
and in accordance with social values (Floridi, Cowls, 2019). AI models learn from 
data that often reflects existing social inequalities. Without an interdisciplinary 
approach, AI can perpetuate and deepen these inequalities in Poland. Experts in 
psychology, social sciences and law help to identify and reduce algorithmic bias 
(Binns, 2018). In addition, companies and government institutions are increasingly 
implementing AI in various fields, such as health, education and finance, which 
require the combination of different scientific disciplines. This interdisciplinary 
approach ensures that these technologies will be tailored to social needs and not 
exclusively for commercial purposes (Dignum, 2019).
4. AI and education: Digital inequalities in Poland are directly related to defi-
ciencies in digital education. Initiatives in this area must cover all levels of educa-
tion in order to prepare the workforce for an AI-based economy. It is also a question 
of implementing a range of programmes for people at risk of losing their jobs as 
a result of production automation processes. To even out the inequalities in access 
to AI, the Polish government is faced with the necessity to increase investment in 
educational programmes that will, on the one hand, develop essential digital skills 
and, on the other hand, enable the acquisition of specialised skills in the field of 
AI. It is particularly important to create accessible courses and programmes that 
will be aimed at different social groups, including the digitally excluded, such as 
foreigners, young people and people of pre-retirement age. Educational initiatives 
will enable a wider circle of citizens to access the opportunities offered by arti-
ficial intelligence. They will also minimise the risk of inequality in terms of the 
skills that are necessary to use AI in the labour market.
5. AI and international collaboration: The activities in this area are aimed at 
supporting the promotion of Polish AI business internationally and supporting the 
development of technologies with respect for human rights in accordance with the 
EU and OECD standards. International cooperation on AI regulation and technol-
ogy exchange can help to level the playing field between Poland and countries that 
are dominant in terms of AI development. Increasing cooperation between coun-
tries, international organisations, and the private sector aims to create global stan-
dards that will ensure more equal access to AI technology worldwide. This kind 
of cooperation is essential to avoid the creation of a digital gap between countries 
with different levels of technological development. Thanks to the above solutions, 
public policies can effectively reduce inequalities related to access to artificial intel-
ligence, promoting the inclusive development of this technology around the world. 
Poland is involved in international initiatives such as the Global Partnership for 


110	
Karolina Olszewska-Ziemba
Artificial Intelligence (GPAI), which promotes the responsible development and 
ethical use of AI worldwide. In addition, Poland participates in European Union re-
search and development programmes such as Horizon Europe, which funds AI-re-
lated projects and supports international cooperation in this area. On a regional 
level, Poland cooperates with the Visegrad Group (V4) countries — the Czech 
Republic, Slovakia and Hungary — to exchange experiences and best practices 
in AI development. In addition, Poland has established bilateral cooperation with 
countries such as Germany and France to jointly develop research and innovation 
projects in the field of AI. Poland’s cooperation with major multinational corpor-
ations is also important. One example is the signing by the Polish side in Febru-
ary 2025 of a memorandum of cooperation with Google aimed at accelerating the 
adoption of AI technology in Poland. This agreement envisages the use of AI to 
drive economic growth and the transformation of strategic sectors for the growth 
and innovation of the Polish economy.
6. AI and the public sector: Inclusive AI development is also being promoted 
through initiatives aimed at supporting the public sector in the implementation 
of AI procurement, better coordination of activities and the development of pro-
grammes such as GovTech Polska. The strategic framework of this programme 
includes references to the e-government strategy in Estonia, which is one of the 
EU leaders in the field of e-government, creating a framework for an inclusive 
civil society. The aim is to engage technology companies in cooperation with 
public institutions so that AI implementations improve the public administration’s 
functioning, including strengthening local government units’s organisational ef-
ficiency, which should be more accessible to citizens. Poland is currently imple-
menting further programmes for the development of the digital economy based on 
the principle of inclusive AI development and, as a result, the reduction of digital 
inequalities. In December 2024, the expert report “Polish Artificial Intelligence 
Development Policy 2025–2030” was published (Ministerstwo Cyfryzacji, 2024), 
which presents a vision of making Poland a global centre for trustworthy AI. The 
expert report confirmed that strategies enabling inclusive AI development must 
be based on such foundations as, firstly, human capital, including in particular the 
development of highly qualified specialists and increasing the availability of AI 
talent; secondly, innovation, which is closely correlated with support for scientific 
research and the use of AI in various areas of the economy, thirdly, investment, 
combining both public and private sector support mechanisms, and fourthly, im-
plementation, consisting of building and then strengthening the infrastructure and 
legal frameworks for the further development of AI in Poland.


Artificial intelligence and digital inequalities: new challenges for Poland	
111
6. Conclusions
Despite progressing digitalisation, Poland struggles with differences in access to 
advanced technology, especially compared to Western European countries. Al-
though Poland is trying to develop its AI strategy with programmes such as the 
Artificial Intelligence Development Strategy in Poland (Ministerstwo Cyfryzac-
ji, 2020), the country still lags behind EU leaders in digital technology, such as 
Sweden, Germany and France. Due to its lower financial resources, less developed 
national digital infrastructure, and a less advanced network of cooperation between 
academia and business, Poland is faced with the challenge of ensuring a more in-
clusive development of AI.
Poland’s main aim should be to reduce digital inequalities regarding access 
to AI technology and redistribution of resources. Therefore, polish programmes 
concerning AI development have to focus on the further development of digital 
infrastructure and access to data. Moreover, it must be highlighted that the na-
tional digital strategy must strongly support local companies in acquiring high-
tech technologies and knowledge in cooperation within the framework of the triple 
helix model. In such a case, polish enterprises will be more able to compete in the 
global AI market. The crucial thing is also to increase the involvement of Polish 
innovative companies in international cooperation programmes in the field of AI. 
It is a strategic move that will enable Poland to acquire knowledge and technol-
ogy from countries that are leaders in the development of AI. As a consequence, 
this should also have a significant impact on reducing digital inequalities in the 
Polish economy.

Abstract: The article deals with the problem of digital inequalities that may develop in Poland due to the wide- spread introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) in all areas of contemporary social and economic life. In addition to the existing forms of digital inequalities, new ones are emerging, related to the dominance of a group of countries with the highest technological level, which are able to effective- ly impose new standards of economic and social development. New forms of digital inequalities, emerging alongside the rapid development of AI, go beyond the traditional issues of Internet con- nectivity or hardware availability. They include disparities in access to the high-quality training data, limited national capacities to develop and deploy large language models (LLMs), unequal availability of high-performance computing infrastructure, and gaps in algorithmic transparency as well as AI governance. The concise analysis presented in this article aims at indicating the strat- egies that Poland has implemented in the third decade of the 21st century to enable the inclusive development of AI at the national level. The research explores how Poland’s national AI strategy can address internal barriers — such as underdeveloped infrastructure, limited computing capacity, and uneven distribution of digital skills — to promote more inclusive and equitable AI develop- ment. The central research question is: What strategic actions should Poland undertake to ensure a more inclusive development of artificial intelligence. The analysis uses a descriptive method to understand the factors that have a particular impact on the occurrence of digital inequalities in Poland. The results of the study show that Poland still faces many technological delays, including those in the implementation of AI solutions. This may result in a deepening of digital inequalities in the sphere of business as well as society. One strategy that seems to have the greatest positive impact on the inclusive development of AI is national and international cooperation between the public and private sectors in this area. 100 Karolina Olszewska-Ziemba
